stem: How did the railroads change mining in the West after the transcontinental line was finished?

stimulus.source_note: A. J. Russell, Golden Spike ceremony, Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869. Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Golden_Spike_ceremony%2C_Promontory%2C_Utah%2C_May_10%2C_1869.jpg
stimulus.text: The photograph shows two locomotives standing nose to nose on a single track at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. A large crowd of workers and officials stands between and around the engines, shaking hands and cheering. One man in the center holds a bottle. The engines face each other where the Union Pacific and Central Pacific tracks met.

options.text: Mining ended, because the railroads carried all the gold and silver east
options.misconception: Background: mining grew after the railroads arrived; the trains carried ore and machinery, they did not end the mines.

options.text: Individual prospectors with picks and pans took over every mine in the West
options.misconception: Background: lone prospectors found the first strikes, but big companies with machines soon took the mines over.

options.text: The railroads banned mining near their tracks to protect the trains
options.misconception: Background: no such ban existed; railroads served mining towns and hauled their ore.

options.text: Big mining companies with heavy machinery replaced lone prospectors

rationales.A: Background: the railroads carried ore out and machinery in, and mining towns boomed along the lines. Mining grew, it did not end.
rationales.B: Background: a lone prospector could stake a claim, but digging deep ore took machines and money. Large companies bought the claims and ran the mines.
rationales.C: Background: railroads ran straight to mining towns like those of the Comstock Lode. They profited from the mines, they did not ban them.
rationales.D: Background from the books: most prospectors never found anything of value, and those who did rarely had the means to work a mine. Large corporations like the Anaconda Copper Mining Company of Butte, Montana, came to dominate mining, working copper, silver, and gold for industry.
rationales.general:
Follow the ore from the ground to the mill.
1. Background: a lone prospector could find a rich vein, but digging it out took drills, pumps, and mills.
2. Background: the railroads hauled that heavy machinery in and hauled ore out, so big companies could work mines a single miner never could.
3. Background: the pick and pan gave way to the corporation and the payroll.
Remember: when the tool gets too big for one person, the business gets bigger too.
